chief_complaint: sharp electric-shock pain in cheek triggered by washing face
hpi_details: 74-year-old female presents with severe, lancinating, 'electric-shock' type pain in her right cheek and jaw. Episodes last a few seconds but are excruciating. They are triggered by washing her face, chewing, or even cold wind. Denies visual changes or jaw claudication.
ideas: She thinks she might have an exposed tooth nerve or a deep root infection that has spread into her jaw.
concerns: She is worried that she will starve and become severely dehydrated because chewing and drinking trigger agonizing pain.
expectations: She hopes to receive a strong numbing medication or nerve painkiller so that she can wash her face and eat a meal.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Trigeminal Neuralgia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Trigeminal Neuralgia: Carbamazepine, monitor LFT/sodium, neurosurgery consult, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp electric-shock pain in cheek triggered by washing face
Key HPI features: severe, brief electric-shock pain in the right cheek and jaw, triggered by washing her face, chewing, or cold wind; she has no visual changes or jaw claudication.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Trigeminal Neuralgia.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Trigeminal Neuralgia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dental pathology without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bilateral pain or young onset.
management_principles: Plan for Trigeminal Neuralgia: Carbamazepine, monitor LFT/sodium, neurosurgery consult
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sharp electric-shock pain in cheek triggered by washing face

74-year-old female presents with severe, lancinating, 'electric-shock' type pain in her right cheek and jaw. Episodes last a few seconds but are excruciating. They are triggered by washing her face, chewing, or even cold wind. Denies visual changes or jaw claudication.
reference_soap.objective: Cranial nerve examination is normal. Sensation to light touch and pinprick on the face is intact. No focal neurological deficits.
reference_soap.assessment: Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux), right V2/V3 distribution.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate Carbamazepine with gradual titration. Monitor CBC and basic metabolic panel (risk of hyponatremia/agranulocytosis). Refer for MRI brain to rule out secondary causes (MS, mass, neurovascular compression).

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Trigeminal Neuralgia
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Trigeminal Neuralgia
Implement evidence-based management plan: Carbamazepine, monitor LFT/sodium, neurosurgery consult

teaching.one_liner: Vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root causing electric-shock cheek pain triggered by light touch, like washing the face.

must_ask.say: Does the pain feel like an electric shock?
Does washing your face trigger it?
How long does each episode last?

history.answer: I came in because I keep getting sudden, excruciating electric-shock pains shooting across my right cheek and jaw.
It started about two weeks ago completely out of nowhere, and the pain strikes instantaneously like a bolt of electricity.
The pain is strictly on the right side of my face, across my right cheek and down along my lower jaw.
It feels like an intense, sharp electric jolt or stabbing needle.
When an attack hits, it is easily a 10 out of 10 in severity. It is so agonizing that I freeze in place.
Each burst lasts only a few seconds, maybe five to ten seconds at most, and then it stops immediately.
In between the shocks, the pain vanishes completely and my face feels totally normal.
I get several attacks every day, and they have been happening more often over the past week.
It is triggered whenever I wash my face, chew food, brush my teeth, or even when a cold breeze blows on my cheek.
Nothing stops the shock once it fires, but keeping my face warm and avoiding touching my cheek prevents attacks.
No, I have not had any facial swelling, skin rash, red eye, or tearing on that side.
No, my vision has been completely normal with no blurring or double vision.
No, my jaw does not ache or get tired when I chew; it only hurts when chewing triggers one of those electric jolts.
No, I do not have headaches, temple tenderness, or soreness when brushing my hair.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I have not noticed any weight loss, though I eat cautiously because I am afraid of triggering a zap.
No, I have not had any weakness, numbness, or tingling in my face or anywhere else in my body.
No, the pain has never occurred on the left side of my face.
I went to my dentist last week thinking it was a bad tooth, but my dental exam and X-rays were completely normal.
I have never experienced anything like this before in my life.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen, but it did not help the pain at all.
It has been awful because I am terrified to wash my face or chew my food normally.
I thought maybe a deep tooth nerve went bad or an infected root in my jaw is flaring up.
I'm terrified that I won't be able to eat or drink anything and will end up starving because the pain is so excruciating.
I just hope you can prescribe a strong pain medicine to numb this cheek so I can wash my face and eat without crying.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or multiple sclerosis.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, regular over-the-counter medicines, or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have a small glass of wine on rare social occasions.
I am a retired schoolteacher, and I live comfortably at home with my husband.
No one in my family has had severe facial nerve pain or neurological disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing elderly female in no acute distress, speaking comfortably but cautious about moving her right cheek.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact, with symmetric facial movements, intact corneal reflexes, and no motor deficits.
Facial sensation to light touch and pinprick is intact and symmetric across the V1, V2, and V3 distributions without sensory loss.
No tenderness elicited on palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Oral mucosa is pink and moist without ulcerations; dentition is intact with no obvious caries, gingival erythema, or swelling.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; conjunctivae are clear without redness, tearing, or discharge.
External auditory canals are clear and tympanic membranes are pearly gray bilaterally without vesicles or inflammation.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 motor strength in all four extremities and symmetric deep tendon reflexes.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
